caseno:
Civil Appeal No. 273 of 2009.
(Arising out of Civil Petition No. 1230 of 2008)
lawyer:
AM Aminuddin, AG with Mohammad Saiful Alam, AAG instructed by Haridas Paul, Advocate-on-Record—For the Appellants. 
Md Asrarul Hoque, Advocate instructed by Md Taufique Hossain, Advocate-on-record—For the Respondent.

Government of Bangladesh represented by the secretary, Ministry of Forest, Bangladesh Secretariat and others ------- Appellants
VS

full_judgment:
Md Ashfaqul Islam, J: This civil appeal by leave is directed against the order dated 7-4-2008 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in Miscellaneous Case No. 21 of 2008 disallowing the miscellaneous case. 

 2. Short facts are that the respondent herein as petitioner filed Administrative Tribunal Case No. 256 of 1994 under section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 against the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Forest and two others for declaration that the order dated 27-6-1992 passed, by the opposite party No.3, the Deputy Chief Conservator, Dhaka removing him from service and the order dated 10-3-1994 issued by the opposite party No. 2, the Chief Conservator of Forest, Dhaka rejecting his departmental appeal are illegal, void, without jurisdiction and of no legal effect and to direct the opposite parties to reinstate him in service with arrear salary and other attending benefits. 

 4. The opposite party No.3 therefore, issued notice upon the petitioner asking him to show cause as to why he would not be dismissed from the service. The petitioner submitted his second written statement of defence pleading innocence. But the authority without considering his reply passed the impugned order removing the petitioner from service. He preferred depart-mental appeal to the opposite party No.2 which was rejected on 10-3-1994 and hence the case was filed on 28-8-1994. 

 5. The opposite parties contested the case by filing a written statement denying the material allegations made in the petition stating, inter alia, that the petition is not maintainable and the petitioner has no cause of action. 

 6. The defence case, in a nutshell, is that the charge of desertion has been proved against the petitioner in the departmental inquiry and, as such, he was removed from service. There was no illegality or irregularity in the departmental proceeding. The impugned order is quite perfect and legal. It does not deserve interference by the Tribunal. The petition is totally misconceived and, as such, it is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

 7. The Administrative Tribunal allowed the case. Against which the present appellants preferred appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. The appeal was dismissed for default on 26-2-2008. The appellants preferred an application for restoration of the said appeal which was also rejected. 

 11. On the other hand Mr Md Asrarul Hoque, the learned Advocate for the respondent supporting the impugned order of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal as well as the Administrative Tribunal contends that the appointment of the Inquiry Officer by the Opposite Party No. 3 in the Charge-sheet in violation of the Rule 7(2)(c) of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985 shows the pre-determination of the Appellant No.3 to impose major penalty of removal from Service and the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka considering such aspect allowed the case, thus the appeal is liable to be dismissed. 

 14. On appreciation of the argument of the parties it is felt by us that the core question that has to be addressed in this Civil Appeal is that whether the Administrative Appellate Tribunal could disallow the Miscellaneous application for restoration of an appeal filed under rule 6(7) of the Administrative Tribunal Rules, 1982 for setting aside the order dated 26-2-2008 dismissing the appeal for default. 

 "Subject to the other provisions of this Act, a Tribunal shall, for the purpose of hearing an application or appeal, as the case may be, follow such procedure as may be prescribed: 

 20. In the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Nurul Alam: 65 DLR (AD) 77 it has been observed: 

 "The point at issue was considered in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 43 of 2010. In the said case after considering the relevant provisions of the Act, 1980, namely: sections 5, 6 and 12 and rules, 6 and II of the Rules, 1982, this Division held that:— 

 From a close study of the above mentioned provisions of the Act as well as the Rules, it appears to us that no period has been prescribed for filing an application for setting-aside an order of dismissal of an appeal, so the question of rejection of an application on the ground of limitation does not arise at all. But, unfortunately the Administrative Appellate Tribunal has failed to consider this legal aspect of the case in passing the impugned order. The Appellate Tribunal has also not stated the provisions of law under which the appellant was required to file an application for restoration within a specified time when it mentioned that the application was filed out of time by 7 (seven) days. What appears to us is that an Administrative Tribunal or the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, as the case may be, may reject an application for setting-aside an order of dismissal or an ex-parte order even if the same is filed within the shortest possible period, if the applicant or the appellant fails to give sufficient cause to the satisfaction of the concerned Tribunal for failure to appear when the case or appeal was taken up for hearing. 

 We find no reason to take a different view in this case other than the view taken in the said decided case." 

 22. In the present case we found that the appeal was filed back in the year 2003 before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. But after long laps of time when the matter was fixed for hearing on 26-2-2008 none appeared for appellants. So, it is apparent that the appellant had lost his interest to proceed with the appeal. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed for default. Subsequently, on an application for restoration of the appeal the same was also disallowed as the Administrative Appellate Tribunal did not believe the plea of the learned Counsel of the appellant to have lost his personal case diary to be an acceptable extenuating circumstance. 

 23. To have the restoration Miscellaneous application sustained the learned counsel of the appellant ought to have shown sufficient cause by furnishing supporting documents (here the personal case diary) to satisfy the appellate Court below.
